site.title: Gordon Bailey — Internship Portfolio
site.lede: Everything built this summer, in one place. Six workstreams, from a peer benchmarking engine sellers can screen-share to the instrumentation and UTM plumbing underneath it. Every page follows the same five headings: the problem, what was done, what came out of it, what it does not cover, and what to pick up next.

_comment: One node per page. `parent` nests it; `order` sorts within a parent.
status:  live      — real content, written and reviewed
drafting  — partial content on the page
awaiting  — page exists, content not yet supplied
`needs` is what has to be handed over before the page can be written. It
doubles as the card text while status is `awaiting`, so a blank page never
pretends to be a finished one.
`body` names a file in projects/ to inline as the page content. Omit it and
build.py renders the standard skeleton from `sections`.
sections: Who was stuck, on what, and why it mattered.
The actual work, in order, including what was tried and dropped.
Findings, decisions, shipped artifacts, numbers where there are numbers.
Scope held back deliberately, and the known soft spots.
The first thing the next person should do.

nodes.title: Hackathon
nodes.blurb: Sixteen hackathon projects scored on one scale and tiered into build, validate and park, with an effort estimate from whoever wrote the code.
nodes.h1: Which sixteen hackathon projects deserve a roadmap slot?
nodes.lede: A hackathon produces enthusiasm, not a roadmap. This scores all sixteen projects on GDV impact, churn prevention and feasibility, merges the duplicates, collects an estimate from each owner, and sorts them into four to build now, five to validate in Q3, and five to park with a named unlock.

nodes.title: Customer Intelligence
nodes.blurb: Three strands of one question: how do we tell a customer something true about their own fundraising that they could not work out alone? Two ran independently and found the same gap.
nodes.lede: What customers said they need, what the market already claims to offer, and a working answer to the gap both pointed at.

nodes.title: Fundraising Benchmarking
nodes.blurb: Groups every eligible nonprofit with organizations genuinely like it — same cause, same size — scores it inside that group, and turns the shortfall into a ranked list of levers. 3,161 accounts, 38 peer groups, 73% of variation explained.
nodes.h1: How is this organization really doing?
nodes.lede: Every nonprofit raises a different amount for different reasons. This compares each one against organizations genuinely like it — same cause, same size — and turns the difference into a short list of what to try next.

nodes.title: Competitive Intelligence
nodes.blurb: Nine vendors, eight AI launches in twelve months, every claim graded on its evidence. Trust language has converged across the market; verifiability is unclaimed by all nine.
nodes.h1: What nine competitors ship, claim, and never mention
nodes.lede: Every vendor in the category now says “we have AI”, which makes the marketing useless as a signal. This separates what has shipped from what is only announced, dates the landscape onto one timeline, and marks the evidence strength on every cell.

nodes.title: Customer Interview Synthesis
nodes.blurb: 39 admin interviews across 33 organizations. The unmet need is AI that is controllable, explainable and measurable. Reporting turned out to be the largest pain cluster in the dataset.
nodes.h1: What 39 admins said about AI, reporting and insights
nodes.lede: Everyone agrees customers want AI. Nobody could say which AI, or why the AI already shipped was not being adopted. This synthesises 39 interviews across 33 organizations, nine workflow personas and all five segments.

nodes.title: Instrumentation
nodes.blurb: A two-layer measurement framework for Pro admin: a lagging health scoreboard, and leading per-workflow instrumentation across eight areas where every KPI names the decision it informs.
nodes.h1: How would we know if the admin experience got better?
nodes.lede: Pro had health metrics and almost no early signal on any specific workflow, and no agreed definition of “active admin” — so two people could report different activation numbers from the same database and both be right.

nodes.title: UTM
nodes.blurb: Twelve Jira tickets across two epics, the ten-hop chain UTM has to survive, and every linked Confluence page, Figma file and PR pulled from the tickets. Five ticket statuses had moved since the programme map was drawn.
nodes.h1: Making UTM survive the whole donation stack
nodes.lede: Marketing attribution was broken end to end: some Studio URLs carried UTMs, nothing persisted them to the transaction, and nothing surfaced them in reporting or the API. This maps the programme with every status verified against Jira rather than the slide.

nodes.title: Guides
nodes.blurb: Two attempts to make something reusable by someone who was not here: one mapping 1,202 repositories, one turning 24 non-functional requirements into questions a PM can ask.
nodes.lede: Written so the next person does not have to reconstruct any of this from scratch, and honest enough about their own limits to be safe to trust.

nodes.title: Non-Functional Guide
nodes.blurb: The 24 requirements that decide whether a release survives production, each with the questions to ask engineering and the spec language to write down, plus a 53-item release-readiness process and a rotating Release Lead role.
nodes.h1: The qualities that decide whether a release survives production
nodes.lede: A working feature answers “what does it do?” Everything that decides whether it holds up — speed, reliability, safety, and the cost of changing it later — sits in a vocabulary most product managers were never taught. This is the translation layer.

nodes.title: Data Architecture Repo Guide
nodes.blurb: 1,202 repositories mapped into ten clusters, four journeys traced end to end, a decision tree for “where do I look?” and a triage tool for “what broke?”, with ownership labelled documented, inferred or contested.
nodes.h1: Where do I look, in 1,202 repositories?
nodes.lede: A product manager gets told something is broken and faces the whole GitHub org with no map. This is an orientation map built from repository metadata, and it says so on every screen.

nodes.title: Corporate Strategy
nodes.blurb: Two gaps and five findings that size them, taken to Amplitude rather than accepted on their face.
nodes.lede: The growth argument the project work sits underneath. Both gaps are versions of the same problem: the platform monetises moments of generosity but does not build generous people.

nodes.title: How to Grow GDV
nodes.blurb: 20% of donors produce 39% of GDV, and half of that sits in the 2-gift band rather than the loyal tail. The concentration analysis, the per-donor slope, and what one more gift is worth.
nodes.lede: Repeat donors are 20% of donors producing 39% of GDV, a 1.9× over-index. The money sits in the shallow end of the frequency curve, not the tail.

nodes.title: How Do We Acquire Better Donors?
nodes.blurb: “Better” defined as likely to return, then measured: a 12.3% baseline repeat rate, a median 23-day window, and roughly $36M a year per percentage point of lift.
nodes.h1: How do we acquire better donors?
nodes.lede: A better donor is one who gives again, because a second gift nearly doubles annual value and can be measured in 90 days rather than a year.

nodes.title: How Do We Build Better Relationships With Super Donors?
nodes.blurb: Four mechanics aimed at the 2-gift band: an owner, a Braze programme in the 23-day window, the Giving Conference as research, and Giving Wrapped.
nodes.h1: How do we build better relationships with super donors?
nodes.lede: 7.1 million people produce 39% of GDV and receive the same experience as a first-time donor. The programme belongs at the second gift, where 4.9M people and $871M already sit.

nodes.title: How Do We Make Giving Cool?
nodes.blurb: Chat and copy-link referrals return at 27–28%; organic social returns at 10.6%, below platform average. The answer is in-person community events with the donation captured in the room.
nodes.h1: How do we make giving cool?
nodes.lede: Coolness has to be borrowed from somewhere. The intuitive source is fame. The referral data points at people you already know.
